blocks.text: 1. Confusion Matrix

blocks.alt: Predictions and actual labels together form the confusion matrix grid

blocks.text: Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1 Score, the four topics already covered in this module, each quietly relied on the exact same four underlying categories, True Positives, True Negatives, False Positives, and False Negatives, first previewed briefly back in the Accuracy topic. The Confusion Matrix is the full, formal, dedicated deep dive into that exact four-category grid, the single most complete, most detailed summary of a classifier's performance available, and the foundation every other classification metric in this module is quietly built from.

Understanding the confusion matrix directly, rather than only encountering its four categories piecemeal across separate metric topics, makes every metric already covered considerably easier to reason about, and it sets up the remaining topics in this module, ROC Curve, AUC, Log Loss, Precision-Recall Curve, and Cohen Kappa, all of which build in some way on this same underlying grid.
2. The Structure of the Grid

blocks.alt: The grid has rows for the actual class and columns for the predicted class

blocks.text: A confusion matrix for binary classification is a simple 2 by 2 grid. One axis represents what the model actually predicted, positive or negative, and the other axis represents what the true label actually was, positive or negative. Every possible combination of predicted and actual label defines exactly one cell in this grid.

The cell where the model predicted positive and the true label was actually positive holds the True Positive count. The cell where the model predicted positive but the true label was actually negative holds the False Positive count. The cell where the model predicted negative but the true label was actually positive holds the False Negative count. The cell where the model predicted negative and the true label was actually negative holds the True Negative count, exactly the same four categories already introduced in the Accuracy topic, now given a proper visual structure.

blocks.text: 3. Four Numbers, the Complete Picture

blocks.alt: The confusion matrix holds true positive, false positive, true negative, and false negative

blocks.text: Every single prediction a binary classifier makes, across an entire evaluation dataset, lands in exactly one of these four cells, no more and no fewer. Tallying up how many predictions land in each of the four cells produces four raw counts, and these four counts together represent the single most complete, most detailed picture of a classifier's performance that exists, more complete than any single summary metric could ever be on its own.

This is the key insight worth carrying forward from this topic: every metric already covered in this module, and several more covered in the remaining topics, is simply some specific ratio or combination of these exact same four counts. Rather than four separate, unrelated ideas, Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1 Score are all different lenses looking at the exact same underlying data, the confusion matrix's four cells.
4. Every Prior Metric, Derived Directly from This Grid

It is worth making the connection to every metric already covered in this module completely explicit. Accuracy is True Positives plus True Negatives, divided by the sum of all four cells combined, exactly the formula covered in the Accuracy topic. Precision is True Positives divided by True Positives plus False Positives, using only the top row of the grid, exactly the formula covered in the Precision topic.

Recall is True Positives divided by True Positives plus False Negatives, using only the left column of the grid, exactly the formula covered in the Recall topic. F1 Score is the harmonic mean of Precision and Recall, itself therefore also fully derivable from the same four cells, exactly the formula covered in the F1 Score topic. Every single one of these four metrics, despite feeling like separate, distinct ideas when covered individually, is simply a different arithmetic combination of the exact same four confusion matrix cells.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Recognizing that every classification metric is ultimately just a specific combination of these four numbers is one of the most useful mental models to carry forward through the rest of this module, and it makes learning any new classification metric considerably faster, since the question becomes simply which combination of the same four familiar numbers that new metric uses.

blocks.text: 5. Two Genuinely Different Kinds of Mistakes

blocks.alt: A false positive is a genuinely different mistake than a false negative

blocks.text: The confusion matrix's real diagnostic power comes from separating what a single number like accuracy lumps together: two genuinely different kinds of mistakes a classifier can make. A False Positive is a false alarm, the model predicted positive when the true label was actually negative, exactly the error type covered in depth in the Precision topic, since precision measures how often positive predictions avoid this specific mistake.

A False Negative is a miss, the model predicted negative when the true label was actually positive, exactly the error type covered in depth in the Recall topic, since recall measures how thoroughly genuine positives avoid this specific mistake. These two error types very often carry genuinely different real-world costs, exactly the asymmetric-cost situations already covered concretely in both the Precision and Recall topics, spam filtering favoring low False Positives, disease screening favoring low False Negatives, and the confusion matrix is what makes this distinction visible and countable in the first place.
6. Exposing Error Patterns a Single Number Hides

blocks.alt: A single accuracy number hides which class struggles, while the confusion matrix reveals the real pattern

blocks.text: Raw accuracy, reported as a single number, deliberately hides exactly which kind of mistake a model tends to make, lumping False Positives and False Negatives together into one undifferentiated error count. The confusion matrix exposes this distinction directly, cell by cell, revealing the specific pattern of a model's mistakes rather than just their total quantity.

A model that only ever produces False Positives and essentially never produces False Negatives has a very specific, immediately visible error pattern in its confusion matrix, a large number in the False Positive cell and a near-zero number in the False Negative cell. A model with the opposite tendency, primarily missing genuine positives rather than raising false alarms, shows the exact opposite, equally visible pattern. This kind of pattern visibility is the confusion matrix's core diagnostic value, something no single summary metric, however well chosen, can fully replace.
7. Beyond Binary: The N by N Confusion Matrix

blocks.alt: A 2 by 2 grid extends into an N by N grid for many classes

blocks.text: The confusion matrix extends naturally beyond binary classification, generalizing to an N by N grid for a problem with N possible classes, one row and one column for every single class in the problem, exactly the multiclass setting already covered for Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1 Score in their own topics. The diagonal cells of this larger grid, where the row and column represent the exact same class, hold the count of correct predictions for each specific class.

The off-diagonal cells reveal something a single accuracy number, even a per-class one, cannot show directly: exactly which class tends to get mistaken for which other specific class. A digit-recognition model that frequently confuses the digit 4 with the digit 9 will show a large number specifically in the cell where the true label is 4 and the predicted label is 9, a specific, actionable confusion pattern invisible in any single aggregate metric.
8. Normalized Confusion Matrices

blocks.alt: Raw counts get normalized into percentages

blocks.text: A confusion matrix reported in raw counts can be genuinely difficult to interpret and compare when different classes have very different numbers of examples, exactly the class imbalance concern already covered in depth in the Accuracy topic. A class with a thousand examples will naturally show much larger raw numbers throughout its row than a class with only ten examples, even if both classes are being classified with comparably good or comparably poor accuracy.

A normalized confusion matrix addresses this directly by converting each row into percentages, dividing every cell in a row by that row's total, so each row sums to 100 percent regardless of how many raw examples that particular class actually contains. This makes normalized confusion matrices directly comparable across classes of very different sizes, ensuring a large class's sheer raw count does not visually dominate or obscure a smaller, but potentially equally important, class's error pattern.

blocks.text: 9. Reading a Confusion Matrix in Practice

A confusion matrix with a strong, dominant diagonal and comparatively weak off-diagonal cells indicates a model performing well overall, with few systematic, repeated error patterns to worry about. A confusion matrix where one specific off-diagonal cell stands out clearly above the others reveals a specific, identifiable, and often genuinely fixable confusion between two particular classes, worth investigating directly, whether through better features that distinguish those two specific classes, or through collecting more training examples of whichever class is being mistaken for the other.

A confusion matrix where an entire row or column looks weak overall, with correct predictions scattered thin across that entire row, indicates the model is failing badly on one particular class specifically, a pattern that a single overall accuracy number, or even an overall F1 Score, could easily mask entirely if that struggling class happens to be a small minority within an otherwise well-performing dataset.
10. Worked Example
The example below computes and displays both a raw and a normalized confusion matrix for a multiclass classifier, directly illustrating how off-diagonal cells reveal specific confusion patterns.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, ConfusionMatrixDisplay
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
# Three classes, with classes 1 and 2 deliberately overlapping to create real confusion
X_class0 = rng.normal(loc=[0, 0], scale=1.5, size=(60, 2))
X_class1 = rng.normal(loc=[5, 5], scale=2.5, size=(60, 2))
X_class2 = rng.normal(loc=[6, 6], scale=2.5, size=(60, 2))  # overlaps heavily with class 1
X = np.vstack([X_class0, X_class1, X_class2])
y = np.array([0] * 60 + [1] * 60 + [2] * 60)

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=42, stratify=y)

model = LogisticRegression()
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
predictions = model.predict(X_test)

raw_matrix = confusion_matrix(y_test, predictions)
normalized_matrix = confusion_matrix(y_test, predictions, normalize='true')

print("Raw confusion matrix:")
print(raw_matrix)
print("\nNormalized confusion matrix (row percentages):")
print(np.round(normalized_matrix, 2))
print("\nNotice classes 1 and 2 likely show meaningful off-diagonal confusion, reflecting their overlap")

blocks.content: ConfusionMatrixDisplay, imported alongside confusion_matrix, can render this grid as an actual visual heatmap in a real notebook environment, making off-diagonal confusion patterns even easier to spot at a glance than scanning raw numbers.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: The Confusion Matrix is a grid crossing predicted label against actual label, defining four cells: TP, TN, FP, and FN.
Every metric covered earlier in this module, Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1 Score, is a specific combination of these four numbers.
It separates False Positives, false alarms, from False Negatives, misses, two genuinely different kinds of mistakes.
It exposes specific error patterns that a single summary number necessarily hides or averages away.
It extends to an N by N grid for multiclass problems, with off-diagonal cells revealing exactly which classes get confused with which.
Normalizing each row into percentages makes the matrix fairly comparable across classes of very different sizes.
A strong diagonal signals good performance; a standout off-diagonal cell or a weak row reveals a specific, actionable problem.
Understanding this grid directly makes every classification metric in this module easier to reason about and connect together.
Next up: Log Loss, which moves beyond hard predicted labels to evaluate the quality of a model's predicted probabilities directly.
